conversation.content: Let's design a URL shortener. But before you start drawing boxes — why? Why would a company build this internally instead of using bit.ly?

Great question. There are three strong reasons for building in-house. First, data ownership — every shortened URL represents a customer touchpoint. With bit.ly, they see your click data, your customer geography, your marketing campaign performance. That's competitive intelligence you're handing to a third party. Second, reliability dependency — if bit.ly goes down, all your marketing links, email links, and SMS links are dead. You've outsourced a critical part of your customer journey to a vendor's SLA. Third, customization — branding (yourcompany.co/deal), integration with internal analytics, custom redirect logic (A/B testing different landing pages), and compliance controls for regulated industries where you need audit trails on every redirect.
Okay, but bit.ly costs $35/month for a business plan. Building and maintaining a custom service costs — what, $500K per year in engineering time plus infrastructure? How do you justify that to a CFO?

The bit.ly comparison is misleading at scale. Their enterprise plan for high volume is $300K+ per year. But more importantly, the real ROI isn't in the shortening — it's in the data platform it enables. An internal URL shortener becomes the company's link intelligence layer. Every customer click across every channel — email, SMS, social, ads — flows through your system. You know which campaigns drive engagement, which users click what, which geographies respond to which offers. That click-stream data feeds your recommendation engine, your marketing attribution model, and your customer 360 profile. The URL shortener costs $500K but the data it generates drives $10M in better-targeted marketing spend. That's the pitch to the CFO: it's not a URL shortener, it's a customer behavior capture system.
Now you're talking. That's the VP answer. Let's say the CFO is convinced. Walk me through the product roadmap — what's in v1, v2, v3?

V1 — 6 weeks: Core shortening and redirect. REST API, branded domains, basic click counting. This replaces bit.ly and stops the data leakage immediately. Target: marketing team as first internal customer. V2 — quarter 2: Analytics dashboard with click-through rates, geographic breakdown, device breakdown, time-series views. A/B testing support — same short URL redirects to different landing pages based on rules. API for programmatic link creation so product teams can generate links in email templates. V3 — quarter 3-4: Real-time click stream published to Kafka for downstream consumers. Deep link support for mobile apps. Link-level fraud detection (click bots, inflated metrics). Self-service portal for all teams to create and manage their own branded domains. Integration with the company's identity platform for authenticated click tracking.
Good roadmap. Now let's get technical. But I want you to design for the v3 vision, not just v1. Architecture that scales to where we're headed.

The architecture serves two purposes: fast redirects and rich data capture. For the redirect path: CDN layer handles the hottest links at the edge — branded domain DNS points to our CDN. Cache miss goes to a global load balancer, then to regional redirect servers. These are stateless, fast — they look up the short code in Redis (primary) or the database (fallback), execute any A/B testing rules, log the click event, and return a 302 redirect. For the data capture path: every redirect emits a click event to Kafka — containing the short code, timestamp, user agent, IP, referer, and any cookies. A stream processing layer (Flink or Spark Streaming) enriches the events — IP to geo, user agent to device type — and writes to a click analytics store (ClickHouse for time-series analytics) and to the company's data lake for downstream consumption. The link management layer is a separate service — CRUD operations for links, A/B testing configuration, domain management — backed by PostgreSQL.
You mentioned A/B testing on redirects. How does that work technically? And more importantly — how does the marketing team configure it without filing an engineering ticket?

The short URL maps to a 'link config' rather than a single destination. The config specifies: default destination, and optionally, an experiment with variants. Each variant has a destination URL and a traffic weight (e.g., 50% to landing page A, 50% to landing page B). The redirect server reads the config, hashes the request (using a consistent hash of user cookie or IP for sticky assignment), and routes to the appropriate variant. For self-service: a web UI where marketing creates a link, toggles 'A/B test,' adds variant URLs and weights. Previews show the expected distribution. Results are visible in the analytics dashboard — click-through rate, conversion rate (if we have a conversion pixel), bounce rate per variant. When the experiment concludes, they click 'pick winner' and all traffic routes to the winning variant. No code changes, no deploys, no engineering tickets.
How does this make money? Or rather — how does this become a profit center rather than a cost center?

Three revenue angles. First, internal cost savings: marketing teams currently pay for multiple tools — bit.ly for link management, Mixpanel for click analytics, Optimizely for A/B testing. This platform replaces portions of all three. At a large company, that's easily $500K-1M in annual SaaS savings. Second, marketing efficiency: better click attribution directly improves ad spend ROI. If the data shows that SMS links convert 3x better than email links for a specific segment, the marketing team shifts budget accordingly. Even a 5% improvement in a $100M marketing budget is $5M saved. Third, and this is the ambitious play: if we build this well enough, we can offer it as a platform feature to our customers. If we're a SaaS company, our customers want branded short links too. We become the link intelligence layer for our ecosystem, and it becomes a product differentiator that increases platform stickiness.
That's a strong business case. Now let's stress-test the architecture. Black Friday — your biggest marketing push of the year. Traffic is 20x normal. What breaks?

At 20x, the redirect path is probably fine — CDN absorbs most of it, and the redirect servers are stateless and horizontally scalable. We'd pre-scale the server fleet a week before Black Friday based on projected traffic. What breaks: the analytics pipeline. Kafka can handle the throughput, but the stream processing layer (Flink) and the analytics database (ClickHouse) may not be sized for 20x ingestion. ClickHouse insertions back up, dashboards become stale, and marketing can't see real-time campaign performance — which is exactly when they need it most. Mitigation: pre-scale the Flink cluster and ClickHouse nodes. More importantly, decouple the real-time dashboard from the full analytics pipeline. A lightweight real-time counter service (Redis-based) gives marketing their top-line numbers — total clicks, clicks per campaign, clicks per minute — within seconds. The detailed breakdown (geo, device, funnel) can lag by a few minutes.
Security concern. Someone uses your platform to create a short link that redirects to a phishing site. Your branded domain is now associated with a scam. How do you handle this?

Multi-layered defense. At creation time: scan the destination URL against known malware and phishing databases — Google Safe Browsing API, PhishTank. Block links to known bad destinations. For internal-only platforms, require authentication to create links, which creates accountability. Post-creation: continuous re-scanning of destination URLs because a legitimate page can be compromised after the link is created. If a destination becomes flagged, automatically disable the link and redirect to a warning page. At redirect time: if the destination is suspicious but not confirmed malicious, show an interstitial page — 'You are about to leave [company] and visit [domain]. Continue?' Operationally: a report abuse mechanism — any user who encounters a suspicious link can flag it for review. A security team reviews flagged links and can instantly disable them. And monitor for bulk creation — rate limit link creation per account to prevent mass phishing campaigns.
Last topic. You're presenting this to the executive team for budget approval. Give me the 60-second elevator pitch.

Every time a customer clicks a link from us — in an email, SMS, ad, or social post — we lose that data to a third party. We're paying bit.ly to see our own customer behavior. I'm proposing we build an internal link intelligence platform. V1 ships in 6 weeks, replaces bit.ly, and immediately stops the data leakage. V2 gives marketing real-time analytics and A/B testing on every link, eliminating $500K in redundant tooling. V3 feeds click-stream data into our data lake, improving marketing attribution and potentially saving millions in ad spend. The investment is $500K per year. The returns are $1M in tool consolidation, measurable improvement in marketing ROI, and a strategic data asset that compounds in value as we scale. We're not building a URL shortener — we're building the nervous system of our customer engagement pipeline.
You'd get my budget approval. Excellent interview — you think about systems as business enablers, not just technical solutions. That's what we need at the VP level. Thank you.

strengths: Exceptional business acumen — justified the technical investment with concrete ROI
Strong product thinking — phased roadmap with clear customer value at each stage
Compelling executive communication — the elevator pitch was persuasive and well-structured
weaknesses: Capacity estimation was absent — no QPS calculations, storage sizing, or cost modeling
Database design was mentioned briefly but not explored — no schema discussion
Technical depth was sacrificed for business breadth — some areas were surface-level
